Being. The most fundamental concept in metaphysics and ontology—the abstract quality of existing or having reality. Being is philosophy's most elusive and essential topic. Heidegger made the question of Being itself central to philosophy, asking what it means to be rather than simply assuming the answer.

Heidegger reversed metaphysical tradition by making the question of Being the foundation of all philosophy. Most philosophers assume what Being is rather than asking the question. For Heidegger, Being is not a thing but the condition enabling intelligibility. Being is revealed through human existence—through Dasein, whose fundamental mode is being-in-the-world.

This was a radical shift from earlier thinking. Parmenides, the pre-Socratic ancient Greek philosopher, had argued that "Being is" and "Non-being is not," making Being eternal, unchanging, indivisible, and absolute. That was already a challenge to common sense and it became foundational to Western metaphysics. Later, Neoplatonism developed a hierarchical metaphysics of being emanating from the One—the transcendent, ineffable source—followed by the divine intellect, the world-soul, and physical matter.

A key distinction central to ontology is between Being itself and beings—abstract existence or intelligibility versus concrete existing things. Medieval philosophers struggled with this distinction. Heidegger's concept of Being differs from traditional metaphysics in an important way: he treats Being as a dynamic process of revealing-and-concealing, which he called aletheia. This contrasts with traditional substance metaphysics, which treats Being as static presence. Contemporary debates now explore whether Being is a univocal concept applicable to all existing things or an equivocal term used differently across domains of reality.
